notes: \cpara{Recalls Asch's finding that one fellow dissenter sharply reduces conformity, and says joining a lone rebel feels glorious.}

\cpara{The factual core of the essay, and it reports half the result. Being the first to dissent was harder, as the essay says: facing a unanimous wrong majority, Asch's lone subjects went along ``in 36.8 per cent of the selections,'' about four times as often as with an ally. But they gave the correct, dissenting answer in the other 63 per cent, and about one quarter ``never agreed with the erroneous judgments of the majority.'' Lonely dissent was the most common response. The essay keeps the difficulty and drops the fact that most people managed it. ``Experiment shows'' appears twice in two paragraphs, and the experiment shows less than the essay says.}
\cpara{Contrasts the two: dissenting alone feels like wearing a clown suit to school, not like wearing black.}
\cpara{The author's dislikes, offered as a premise (``you may have noticed this''). ``Everyone wants to be an iconoclast'' is a claim about everyone, with no support.}

\cpara{Vegetarians are respected for courage the author ``expects'' it takes, a guess about other people's inner lives. The paragraph builds a scale on which the author's own cause, cryonics, will be placed at the top two paragraphs later.}
\cpara{Explains that people think they understand a vegetarian's motives, so even if they disagree they know how to relate.}
\cpara{Argues that wearing black to school is a recognized, standard kind of rebellion that challenges no one to think anything new.}

\cpara{The essay's real subject arrives: cryonics. The highest example of lonely courage is the author's own cause (an inference from later writing: in ``Normal Cryonics,'' 19 January 2010, the author wrote ``If you don't sign up your kids for cryonics then you are a lousy parent''). The paragraph never considers that people who find cryonics strange may simply judge that it will not work. Their side is written as noises: ``Huh? What? Are you crazy?'' The reader is invited to laugh at people the essay has not let speak.}

\cpara{Announced as a temptation, then given in full, and the next paragraph builds on it (``probably didn't serve its bearers as well''). Calling a story post facto does not license relying on it. No evidence is given that lone exiles died, that the fear exists, or that it is inherited. The disclaimer ``that is not the nature of evolutionary psychology'' appears here and again, nearly word for word, in the next paragraph.}

\cpara{The essay's boldest claim, that ``the fear of thinking really different is stronger than the fear of death,'' rests on one comparison: more people skydive than sign up for cryonics. The comparison is rigged. A skydive is one purchase with a known result. Cryonics cost ``\$28,000 to \$200,000'' in the United States as of 2011 (Wikipedia, ``Cryonics''), and no one has been revived. Cost and doubt explain low sign-up at least as well as fear. The essay mentions neither.}
\cpara{Says even that is not the highest courage: Robert Ettinger had to be the first to propose cryonics.}

\cpara{The paragraph qualifies itself until little is left: revolution is ``not the only route,'' ``rare even among the great,'' cannot be sought, and needs ``all the power and wisdom'' of existing knowledge plus ``a dose of sheer luck.'' What remains is that a correct person who finds something new must then be brave. The essay has moved from cryonics to scientific revolution without arguing that the one belongs with the other. The placement does the work.}
\cpara{Calls this first-person dissent the true courage that rock bands try to fake.}
\cpara{Admits that not everything courageous is wise, like walking off a cliff.}

\cpara{The footnote cites Robin Hanson's ``Against Free Thinkers'' (14 June 2007) for a small point. Hanson's post argues against the essay's thesis: ``Contrary to their self-image, undiscriminating freethinkers are our main obstacle to innovation.'' On his account, good odd ideas are held back less by fear of dissent than by the crowd of careless dissenters they must be told apart from. The essay cites it for a smaller point, agrees with it in its last paragraph (dissent is ``just a bias either way''), and does not apply it to cryonics.}

\cpara{The rule stated here sits uneasily with the essay's emphasis. If one should differ only with ``an overwhelmingly good reason,'' then the reason is what matters, not the courage. The essay gave courage most of its length and gives the reason two sentences.}
\cpara{Grants that some real iconoclasts and tolerant communities exist, and more people imagine themselves rebels than are, but scientific revolutionaries are far rarer still.}

\cpara{The irony (``you see,'' ``totally'') gives cover, but the next paragraph confirms that dissenting too easily is ``my own nature.'' The author claims a place among the rare people the previous paragraph described, and the evidence offered is that the author's serious conversations were with books. The essay's own mark of genuine dissent, a cost paid in public, is not applied to its author.}
\cpara{Warns that finding dissent easy means you must guard against dissenting too readily, since others have reasons; being a free thinker is a bias, not a virtue.}
